title: Death and life, to test
hook: He created death and life to test which of you is best in deed (67:2)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the surah before sleep, al-Mulk, and your line, it intercedes. Did a few verses come before your phone last night? Today, its second verse. Day six hundred thirty-seven, the end of a week.

Say it out loud: life and death. That's the order everyone uses. Birth first, then the end. It's the order of a biography, a gravestone, a hospital chart. Now read the second verse of al-Mulk, and something is backwards. The Qur'an says Allah created death and life. Death first. It's not a slip. And then, in the same breath, it tells you why both were made, and the answer isn't what most people expect. It's not about how much you do.

Al-Mulk, verse two, in Pickthall's translation: "Who hath created life and death that He may try you which of you is best in conduct; and He is the Mighty, the Forgiving." Notice Pickthall turns it into the familiar order, life and death. The Arabic says al-mawt wa al-hayah: death, then life. Commentators offered reasons. Some say death is named first because it's the thing people forget, and remembering it changes how the life gets lived. Others say death came first in the sense that every person was nothing, lifeless, before they were given life. The Qur'an doesn't say which; it just puts death in front. Then the purpose: to test you, which of you is ahsanu 'amalan. Best in deed. Not most in deed. Not the longest list, the busiest calendar, the most prayers stacked up. Best. An early scholar of Mecca, al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, is reported to have explained best as the most sincere and the most correct: done for Allah, and done the right way. One without the other doesn't count as best. And the verse closes with two names together: the Mighty, the Forgiving. The test is real, and so is the mercy. The one who sets it can't be fooled and also forgives. Put the whole verse on an ordinary day. You don't have to do everything. Death is coming for everyone, so the question isn't how much time is left. It's what one thing, done today, could be done well, and for the right reason.
screen: `BEST IN DEED, NOT MOST IN DEED.`

segments.voice: The practice: do one excellent deed. Sit, and look at today's list, the real one in your head. Pick one item, ordinary is fine: a meal, a reply, a chore, a prayer. Ask two questions. Why am I doing it? And how would it look done well? Picture doing it that way, start to finish, with nothing rushed. Then, once the bell ends, go and do that one thing as the best version, not the fastest. The bell holds the time.
Death and life. In 67:2 Allah creates death, then life, to test which of you is best in deed: most sincere, most correct, not most. Today's word.

Your line: best in deed. This week walked from as much as you can, through part with kindness, a way out, turning back sincerely, a house near you and it intercedes, to here. Today, do one thing best, not most. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims often cite 67:2 to say that what matters before Allah is the quality of a deed, done sincerely and correctly, rather than its quantity; many recite the verse as part of al-Mulk each night.

fork.setup: you have one free hour and a long list of good things you could do. by 67:2, what does the test look at?
fork.reveal: best in deed, not most. al-Fudayl is reported to have said: the most sincere and the most correct.

original.note: Arabic, 67:2: best in deed. ahsan, best, most excellent; 'amal, deed, work.

trapdoor: what you thought: life is a test.
what it means: death and life were made to show who is best in deed, not who does most.
what a scholar hears: the Arabic puts al-mawt before al-hayah, and al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad glossed ahsanu 'amalan as most sincere, most correct.

sources.ref: saying of al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad on ahsanu 'amalan, reported in classical tafsir (e.g. al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir)

notes: Pickthall wording of 67:2 quoted from memory; please confirm. Pickthall's 'life and death' reverses the Arabic order, which the script points out.
The two reasons commentators give for death being named first are summarized; confirm both appear in classical tafsir.
Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad's gloss (akhlasuhu wa aswabuhu) and his description as 'an early scholar of Mecca' (he settled there) should be confirmed.
